paragraphs.title: The Completion of Creation and the Holiness of the Sabbath

verses.text: Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them.
And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.
And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made.

easy.q: What did God complete after the six days of creation?
answers: The heavens, the earth, and all their host
Only the light
Only the sea
easy.explanation: The passage says that the heavens, the earth, and everything in them were completed.

easy.q: What did God rest from on the seventh day?
answers: All the work he had done
Speaking to the man
Watering the garden
easy.explanation: God ceased from his work of creation on the seventh day.

easy.q: What did God do to the seventh day?
answers: He blessed it and made it holy
He hid it
He called it the first day
easy.explanation: The seventh day is described as blessed and holy because God rested from his work.

medium.q: Why can we understand that the Sabbath is not merely a break from work, but also a day with special status?
answers: Because the day was blessed and sanctified
Because it was the longest day
Because animals were created on it
medium.explanation: The passage adds blessing and holiness to the cessation of work, giving the day a special significance.

medium.q: What social idea can be inferred from the description of a regular day of rest?
answers: Rest can be part of everyone's way of life
Only kings are allowed to rest
Rest eliminates all responsibility
medium.explanation: A regular day of rest can create a balanced, shared rhythm of life rather than being a privilege reserved for a few.

medium.q: Many ancient cultures had festivals and rituals, but according to the passage, what is distinctive about the status of the seventh day?
answers: It is connected with the completion of creation and God's rest
It was determined by a solar eclipse
It was intended only to celebrate a military victory
medium.explanation: According to the passage, the day's holiness comes from the completion of creation and the cessation of work; comparisons with other cultures require caution and do not prove that the customs were identical.

challenge.q: How might the idea of the Sabbath affect a society in which most people do manual labor?
answers: It could protect a regular time for rest
It requires people to work without stopping
It eliminates the need for laws
challenge.explanation: A regular day of rest could reduce exhaustion and create a social boundary around work, especially in an agricultural or productive society.

challenge.q: What can be inferred from the fact that the passage emphasizes both the completion of the work and the holiness of the day?
answers: Stopping activity is given moral significance
All work is considered evil
Only the result matters, not the process
challenge.explanation: The passage connects completing the work with deliberately stopping, presenting rest as a value rather than merely the absence of activity.

challenge.q: What thought-provoking question arises from the description of God resting from his work?
answers: Is rest a positive part of the order of creation?
Are the heavens made of human material?
Was the earth created by kings?
challenge.explanation: The description invites reflection on planned rest as part of order and meaning, not merely as a response to fatigue.

questions.q: How might the idea of the Sabbath affect a society in which most people do manual labor?
answers: It could protect a regular time for rest
It requires people to work without stopping
It eliminates the need for laws
questions.explanation: A regular day of rest could reduce exhaustion and create a social boundary around work, especially in an agricultural or productive society.

questions.q: What can be inferred from the fact that the passage emphasizes both the completion of the work and the holiness of the day?
answers: Stopping activity is given moral significance
All work is considered evil
Only the result matters, not the process
questions.explanation: The passage connects completing the work with deliberately stopping, presenting rest as a value rather than merely the absence of activity.

questions.q: What thought-provoking question arises from the description of God resting from his work?
answers: Is rest a positive part of the order of creation?
Are the heavens made of human material?
Was the earth created by kings?
questions.explanation: The description invites reflection on planned rest as part of order and meaning, not merely as a response to fatigue.

paragraphs.title: The Creation of Man from the Ground

verses.text: These are the generations of the heavens and of the earth when they were created, in the day that the Lord God made the earth and the heavens,

And every plant of the field before it was in the earth, and every herb of the field before it grew: for the Lord God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was not a man to till the ground.
But there went up a mist from the earth, and watered the whole face of the ground.
And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

easy.q: What was man made from according to the passage?
answers: Stone
Dust from the ground
Water
easy.explanation: God formed man from dust from the ground.

easy.q: What did God breathe into man's nostrils?
answers: The breath of life
A storm wind
Smoke
easy.explanation: The breath of life made man a living soul.

easy.q: Why had the plants of the field not yet grown?
answers: Because it had not rained and there was no man to till the ground
Because it was winter
Because the ground was covered with water
easy.explanation: The passage says that it had not rained and that there was no man to work the ground.

medium.q: In verses 5–7, what does the passage emphasize about man's relationship to the ground?
answers: Man is closely connected to the ground from which he was formed
Man was created from the heavens
The ground is unnecessary to man
medium.explanation: The description connects man with the ground, both as the material from which he was formed and as the place he is to work.

medium.q: What can be inferred from the description of man as someone meant to work the ground?
answers: Man has an active role in the world
Man was meant to avoid all work
Man does not depend on his surroundings
medium.explanation: The passage presents man as active within the world and responsible for caring for the ground.

medium.q: What is a careful reading of the mist rising from the ground?
answers: The passage describes a source of watering within the creation story
The passage proves a specific modern scientific theory
The passage claims that plants do not need water
medium.explanation: The passage may describe a way in which the ground was watered, but it cannot by itself establish a modern scientific theory.

challenge.q: What idea emerges from the combination of dust and the breath of life in the creation of man?
answers: Man is presented as both a material creature and a being with special life
Man is presented as unrelated to the material world
Man is presented as merely a plant
challenge.explanation: The dust represents man's material side, while the breath of life represents the distinctive life given to him.

challenge.q: What can be inferred from the fact that the passage mentions both the absence of man and the work of the ground?
answers: Agriculture is presented as part of man's role in the world
Agriculture is presented as forbidden to man
Plants do not need man at all
challenge.explanation: The wording connects man's presence with working the ground, suggesting that this is a central human role in the description.

challenge.q: What reasonable cultural-historical connection can be explored בעקבות the description of man being formed from the ground?
answers: The importance of land and agriculture in ancient societies
The development of aviation in the ancient world
Space commerce in antiquity
challenge.explanation: Many ancient societies depended on land and water, so the passage invites discussion of humanity's dependence on its agricultural environment without claiming that it originated in a particular text.

questions.q: What idea emerges from the combination of dust and the breath of life in the creation of man?
answers: Man is presented as both a material creature and a being with special life
Man is presented as unrelated to the material world
Man is presented as merely a plant
questions.explanation: The dust represents man's material side, while the breath of life represents the distinctive life given to him.

questions.q: What can be inferred from the fact that the passage mentions both the absence of man and the work of the ground?
answers: Agriculture is presented as part of man's role in the world
Agriculture is presented as forbidden to man
Plants do not need man at all
questions.explanation: The wording connects man's presence with working the ground, suggesting that this is a central human role in the description.

questions.q: What reasonable cultural-historical connection can be explored בעקבות the description of man being formed from the ground?
answers: The importance of land and agriculture in ancient societies
The development of aviation in the ancient world
Space commerce in antiquity
questions.explanation: Many ancient societies depended on land and water, so the passage invites discussion of humanity's dependence on its agricultural environment without claiming that it originated in a particular text.

paragraphs.title: The Garden of Eden and the Trees of the Garden

verses.text: And the Lord God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed.

And out of the ground made the Lord God to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food; the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil.

easy.q: Where did the Lord plant the garden?
answers: In Eden
In Egypt
In the wilderness
easy.explanation: The garden was planted in Eden, to the east, and the man was placed there.

easy.q: Whom did the Lord place in the garden?
answers: The man
Noah
Abraham
easy.explanation: The Lord placed the man he had formed in the garden.

easy.q: Which two special trees are mentioned in the garden?
answers: The tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil
The olive tree and the fig tree
The cedar tree and the palm tree
easy.explanation: The passage mentions the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

medium.q: What does the description of the trees teach us about the garden's purpose for man?
answers: It was intended both for beauty and for food
It was intended only as a hiding place
It was intended only for growing trees
medium.explanation: The trees are described as pleasant to look at and good for food, so the garden provides both beauty and nourishment.

medium.q: What can be inferred from the phrase “out of the ground” about the garden's relationship to the natural world?
answers: The garden is described as part of the natural creation
The garden is described as being made only of stones
The garden is described as a place without plants
medium.explanation: The plants grow from the ground, connecting the garden with the natural world and vegetation.

medium.q: Why might the location of the two special trees inside the garden be significant literarily?
answers: It emphasizes that they are central to the story
It proves that the garden was outside Eden
It shows that there were no other trees in the garden
medium.explanation: Their placement in the garden, together with their distinctive description, emphasizes their importance to what follows.

challenge.q: Many ancient cultures used royal gardens to symbolize abundance and order. How does the passage's description of the garden fit this idea?
answers: It is described as a place of beauty, food, and abundance
It is described as a place of war and scarcity
It is described as a place without vegetation
challenge.explanation: The description of the trees as pleasant to look at and good for food fits the image of a blessed and ordered place, though it does not mean that all cultures described gardens in the same way.

challenge.q: What is the central conceptual tension created by the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil together?
answers: Between continued life and knowledge or moral discernment
Between agriculture and trade
Between city and village
challenge.explanation: The names of the trees place the idea of life alongside the idea of knowledge and distinguishing good from evil.

challenge.q: If all the trees are described as good for food, why do you think two special trees are mentioned separately?
answers: To suggest that they have a role beyond providing food
To say that they were the only trees in the garden
To show that the man could not see them
challenge.explanation: Distinguishing them from the other trees suggests that they are especially important conceptually and narratively, not merely as sources of food.

questions.q: Many ancient cultures used royal gardens to symbolize abundance and order. How does the passage's description of the garden fit this idea?
answers: It is described as a place of beauty, food, and abundance
It is described as a place of war and scarcity
It is described as a place without vegetation
questions.explanation: The description of the trees as pleasant to look at and good for food fits the image of a blessed and ordered place, though it does not mean that all cultures described gardens in the same way.

questions.q: What is the central conceptual tension created by the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil together?
answers: Between continued life and knowledge or moral discernment
Between agriculture and trade
Between city and village
questions.explanation: The names of the trees place the idea of life alongside the idea of knowledge and distinguishing good from evil.

questions.q: If all the trees are described as good for food, why do you think two special trees are mentioned separately?
answers: To suggest that they have a role beyond providing food
To say that they were the only trees in the garden
To show that the man could not see them
questions.explanation: Distinguishing them from the other trees suggests that they are especially important conceptually and narratively, not merely as sources of food.

paragraphs.title: The River and Its Four Branches

verses.text: And a river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from thence it was parted, and became into four heads.
The name of the first is Pison: that is it which compasseth the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold;
And the gold of that land is good: there is bdellium and the onyx stone.
And the name of the second river is Gihon: the same is it that compasseth the whole land of Ethiopia.
And the name of the third river is Hiddekel: that is it which goeth toward the east of Assyria. And the fourth river is Euphrates.

easy.q: What was the initial purpose of the river that flowed from Eden?
answers: To water the garden
To divide the lands
To carry gold from the land
easy.explanation: The river flowed from Eden to water the garden, and only afterward divided into four branches.

easy.q: What was the name of the second river described in the passage?
answers: Pison
Gihon
Euphrates
easy.explanation: The second river was called Gihon.

easy.q: What natural treasures is the land of Havilah described as having?
answers: Gold, bdellium, and onyx
Silver, copper, and iron
Grain, wine, and oil
easy.explanation: The passage mentions good gold, bdellium, and onyx in the land of Havilah.

medium.q: Why is it difficult to identify all the rivers and lands in the passage with certainty on a modern map?
answers: Ancient names may have changed, and the identifications are disputed
The passage does not mention rivers at all
All the rivers certainly disappeared in the Flood
medium.explanation: Place names change over time, and some identifications, such as Havilah and Ethiopia, remain debated in scholarship.

medium.q: Which river in the passage is generally identified with the Tigris?
answers: Gihon
Hiddekel
Pison
medium.explanation: Hiddekel is generally identified with the Tigris River in Mesopotamia, although the biblical identification alone does not establish every detail of the map.

medium.q: What reasonable conclusion follows from the fact that the garden is described as the place from which a river divides into four rivers and where natural treasures are found?
answers: The garden is presented as a source of abundance connected with a wider world
The garden is presented as isolated and lacking resources
The garden is presented as a city built by human beings
medium.explanation: The description of water, gold, and precious stones portrays the garden as a place of abundance, while the rivers connect it with distant lands.

challenge.q: What geographical difficulty arises if the river's description is taken literally as one river dividing into four known rivers?
answers: Known rivers do not currently form such a system from a single source
All rivers in the world always flow from east to west
Rivers have no connection with the lands mentioned
challenge.explanation: The passage describes a common source for four branches, but on a modern map the rivers usually identified as the Tigris and Euphrates do not divide from one source in this way; therefore the map may not be a simple geographical description, or the identifications may be uncertain.

challenge.q: What can cautiously be inferred from mentioning gold, bdellium, and onyx alongside the rivers?
answers: Nature and water are presented as part of the region's abundance
The author describes a specific marketplace and its prices
All these stones are mined only in the wilderness
challenge.explanation: The combination of water, lands, and natural treasures emphasizes the fertility and wealth of the described world, but it provides no information about a particular market or prices.

challenge.q: What important distinction should be made between a religious reading and an attempt to identify the places historically?
answers: The religious meaning can rest on the idea of abundance even without certain geographical identification
If the locations cannot be identified with certainty, the passage has no meaning
Identifying a modern river proves every detail of the creation story
challenge.explanation: The role of the rivers and treasures in the story can be understood even when scholars disagree about the precise locations of all the names.

questions.q: What geographical difficulty arises if the river's description is taken literally as one river dividing into four known rivers?
answers: Known rivers do not currently form such a system from a single source
All rivers in the world always flow from east to west
Rivers have no connection with the lands mentioned
questions.explanation: The passage describes a common source for four branches, but on a modern map the rivers usually identified as the Tigris and Euphrates do not divide from one source in this way; therefore the map may not be a simple geographical description, or the identifications may be uncertain.

questions.q: What can cautiously be inferred from mentioning gold, bdellium, and onyx alongside the rivers?
answers: Nature and water are presented as part of the region's abundance
The author describes a specific marketplace and its prices
All these stones are mined only in the wilderness
questions.explanation: The combination of water, lands, and natural treasures emphasizes the fertility and wealth of the described world, but it provides no information about a particular market or prices.

questions.q: What important distinction should be made between a religious reading and an attempt to identify the places historically?
answers: The religious meaning can rest on the idea of abundance even without certain geographical identification
If the locations cannot be identified with certainty, the passage has no meaning
Identifying a modern river proves every detail of the creation story
questions.explanation: The role of the rivers and treasures in the story can be understood even when scholars disagree about the precise locations of all the names.

paragraphs.title: The Man's Work and the Command in the Garden

verses.text: And the Lord God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
And the Lord God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat:
But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.

easy.q: Why was the man placed in the Garden of Eden?
answers: To work it and keep it
To find the tree of knowledge
To rule over all the animals
easy.explanation: The man was placed in the garden to work it and take care of it.

easy.q: What was the man allowed to eat from the trees of the garden?
answers: Only from the tree of life
From every tree except one
Only from the tree of knowledge
easy.explanation: The man was told that he could eat from every tree of the garden except the tree of knowledge.

easy.q: What warning was given concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil?
answers: The man would be unable to keep the garden
The man would be expelled immediately
The man would die if he ate from it
easy.explanation: Eating from the tree of knowledge was forbidden, and the man was told that he would die if he ate from it.

medium.q: What can be inferred from the fact that the man received both a role and a command?
answers: He was expected to act responsibly and choose how to behave
He was not allowed to do anything in the garden
He was meant only to enjoy the garden
medium.explanation: The work and care entrusted to him give him responsibility, while the command establishes a boundary that he must choose whether to respect.

medium.q: What social idea can be connected with the command in the passage?
answers: A society can grant freedom while also setting boundaries
Every rule eliminates the possibility of choice
Responsibility exists only when there are no prohibitions
medium.explanation: The passage combines broad permission with one focused prohibition, making it relevant to the idea of freedom accompanied by responsibility and limits.

medium.q: In verses 15–17, what does the contrast between permission and prohibition teach about the man's place in the garden?
answers: He is given generous freedom together with a specific responsibility
He is forbidden to enjoy any of the garden's produce
He is given no meaningful choice
medium.explanation: The man may freely eat from every tree except one, so the passage presents both broad freedom and a clear boundary.

paragraphs.title: The Animals and the Naming of the Man

verses.text: And the Lord God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.

And out of the ground the Lord God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them: and whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof.
And Adam gave names to all cattle, and to the fowl of the air, and to every beast of the field; but for Adam there was not found an help meet for him.

easy.q: What did the Lord God say was not good about the man's situation?
answers: That he was alone
That he was in the garden
That he had not named the animals
easy.explanation: The Lord says that it is not good for the man to be alone, and therefore plans to make a suitable helper for him.

easy.q: Why were the animals brought to the man?
answers: So that the man could name them
So that they could build him a house
So that they could teach him to work the ground
easy.explanation: The animals were brought to the man to see what he would call them.

easy.q: What did the man discover after naming the animals?
answers: That he had not found a suitable helper
That all the animals belonged to him
That he could not speak
easy.explanation: At the end of the passage, no suitable helper was found for the man.

medium.q: In verses 18–20, what does the man's naming of the animals show about his role?
answers: He is portrayed as someone who identifies and classifies
He is afraid of all the animals
He is unable to communicate
medium.explanation: Naming presents the man as someone who recognizes, distinguishes, and gives meaning to the world around him.

medium.q: What does the passage's sequence of naming the animals and finding no suitable helper emphasize?
answers: The animals surround the man but do not meet his need for a fitting partner
The man wants to leave the garden, but the animals stop him
The man refuses to name the animals, but God forces him
medium.explanation: Despite his encounter with the animals, the man still does not find a suitable helper.

medium.q: In many ancient cultures, giving a name expressed identity or function. How does that idea fit this passage?
answers: The man names the creatures, portraying him as someone who orders and defines his surroundings
The names are given only to hide the animals
The passage states that all the names came from a particular historical language
medium.explanation: The passage supports the idea that the man sorts and defines his surroundings, but it does not establish the historical language of the names.

challenge.q: What can be inferred from the fact that the man gives names to the animals?
answers: He is portrayed as having the ability to distinguish and classify
He is afraid of all the animals
He is unable to communicate
challenge.explanation: Naming presents the man as someone who recognizes, distinguishes, and gives meaning to the world around him.

challenge.q: What is the central tension in the passage?
answers: The animals are around the man, but they do not meet his need for a suitable partner
The man wants to leave the garden, but the animals prevent him
The man does not want to give names, but God forces him
challenge.explanation: Although the man encounters the animals, he still does not find a suitable helper.

challenge.q: In many ancient cultures, giving a name expressed identity or function. How does that idea fit this passage?
answers: The man names the creatures, portraying him as someone who orders and defines his surroundings
The names are given only to hide the animals
The passage states that all the names came from a particular historical language
challenge.explanation: The passage supports the idea that the man sorts and defines his surroundings, but it does not establish the historical language of the names.

paragraphs.title: The Creation of the Woman and the First Encounter

verses.text: And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof;
And the rib, which the Lord God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man.
And Adam said, This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.

easy.q: What did the Lord God do to the man before taking one of his ribs?
answers: He caused him to fall into a deep sleep
He brought the woman to him
He gave him a new name
easy.explanation: The man fell into a deep sleep, and then one of his ribs was taken.

easy.q: What did the Lord God make from the rib taken from the man?
answers: A city
A woman
An altar
easy.explanation: The rib was made into a woman, who was brought to the man.

easy.q: How did the man describe the woman?
answers: Bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh
A stranger unrelated to him
A queen over all living creatures
easy.explanation: The man emphasized the closeness and shared nature between himself and the woman.

medium.q: In verses 21–23, what does the woman's creation from the man's rib emphasize?
answers: That she is presented as closely connected to the man
That she was created from the ground alone
That she was unrelated to the man
medium.explanation: The account presents the woman as coming from the man, and the man's words emphasize their close connection.

medium.q: What sequence of events is described in the passage?
answers: The man's deep sleep, the taking of the rib, the making of the woman, and her being brought to him
The creation of the woman, the man's sleep, and then the taking of the rib
The naming of the man, the making of the woman, and then the creation of the man
medium.explanation: This is the order of actions described in the passage.

medium.q: What can be inferred from the man describing the woman as “bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh”?
answers: He saw her as a close and essential part of himself
He thought she was merely a weak creature
He did not know who had brought her to him
medium.explanation: The image expresses deep closeness and shared identity rather than alienation.

challenge.q: What social perspective might be reflected in the woman being brought to the man rather than described as coming to him on her own?
answers: The relationship is presented as originating through divine initiative
It establishes that the woman has no will of her own
It describes marriage according to modern law
challenge.explanation: The passage emphasizes the Lord's action in creating and bringing the woman; it does not explicitly state anything about her will or legal status.

challenge.q: In verses 21–23, what does the man's declaration about “bone” and “flesh” communicate about the first encounter?
answers: It presents the meeting as a moment of recognition and closeness
It shows that the man rejects the woman
It shows that the man is indifferent to her
challenge.explanation: The man's words express wonder and recognition of a close relationship, without spelling out every implication of that relationship.

challenge.q: What is the most balanced conclusion from the fact that the man responds with enthusiasm when he sees the woman?
answers: The encounter is presented as a moment of recognizing and welcoming closeness
The man opposes the creation of the woman
The man is indifferent and does not notice the woman
challenge.explanation: The man's words express excitement and recognition of a close connection, but they do not provide a complete account of the relationship's meaning.

questions.q: What social perspective might be reflected in the woman being brought to the man rather than described as coming to him on her own?
answers: The relationship is presented as originating through divine initiative
It establishes that the woman has no will of her own
It describes marriage according to modern law
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes the Lord's action in creating and bringing the woman; it does not explicitly state anything about her will or legal status.

questions.q: In verses 21–23, what does the man's declaration about “bone” and “flesh” communicate about the first encounter?
answers: It presents the meeting as a moment of recognition and closeness
It shows that the man rejects the woman
It shows that the man is indifferent to her
questions.explanation: The man's words express wonder and recognition of a close relationship, without spelling out every implication of that relationship.

questions.q: What is the most balanced conclusion from the fact that the man responds with enthusiasm when he sees the woman?
answers: The encounter is presented as a moment of recognizing and welcoming closeness
The man opposes the creation of the woman
The man is indifferent and does not notice the woman
questions.explanation: The man's words express excitement and recognition of a close connection, but they do not provide a complete account of the relationship's meaning.

paragraphs.title: Unity and Innocence in the Garden

verses.text: Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.

easy.q: What does the man do in relation to his father and mother?
answers: He leaves them
He punishes them
He invites them to the garden
easy.explanation: The passage describes the man as leaving his father and mother.

easy.q: To whom does the man cling?
answers: His brother
His wife
An angel
easy.explanation: The passage says that the man clings to his wife.

easy.q: How are the man and his wife described at the beginning of the passage?
answers: Clothed and afraid
Rich and happy
Naked and unashamed
easy.explanation: They are both naked, but they feel no shame.

medium.q: What might the statement that they will be “one flesh” express?
answers: Deep connection and unity between the couple
A prohibition against starting a family
A life lived separately from each other
medium.explanation: The expression describes a close bond and unity between the man and his wife.

medium.q: Why can leaving one's father and mother be understood as the beginning of a new framework?
answers: Because the couple creates a family relationship of its own
Because the parents disappear from the world
Because the man ceases to be part of society
medium.explanation: The passage presents the couple's relationship as a central bond that creates a new unit.

medium.q: What is the main difference between the man and his wife here and someone who is ashamed of their body?
answers: Here there is no sense of shame or concealment
Here they do not know each other
Here they are wearing formal clothes
medium.explanation: The passage emphasizes that they are naked but are not ashamed.

challenge.q: What social conclusion can be drawn from the movement from parents to wife?
answers: Marriage is presented as a binding and highly important relationship
Parents are no longer important to a person in any situation
Family has no connection to marriage
challenge.explanation: The wording emphasizes that the marital bond creates commitment and a new social unit without saying that the relationship with one's parents is completely abolished.

challenge.q: How can the absence of shame be interpreted conceptually without insisting on a single meaning?
answers: As a state of innocence and mutual acceptance
As proof that they lived in a large city
As a sign that they knew all the laws of society
challenge.explanation: The absence of shame may express innocence, openness, and freedom from fear of exposure; this is a conceptual interpretation, not a proven historical detail.
